title: Adding CSS to a Page
summary: You can add CSS rules to a page in a style element or in a separate CSS file.
introduction: You can add CSS rules to a page in a style element or in a separate CSS file. Start with one colour rule. Then move it to a file so more than one page can use the same style.
learningObjectives: Attach CSS with the style attribute, a style element and a linked stylesheet
Choose the right method for a given situation
Write a correct link element and fix the typical path mistakes

blocks.text: The `style` attribute holds declarations for one element only. There is no selector because the element is already chosen. It is handy for a quick test, for HTML emails (where stylesheets are poorly supported) and for values that JavaScript computes at runtime, such as the width of a progress bar.

blocks.text: For everything else, inline styles are a poor choice. They cannot be reused, so the same declarations get copied onto every similar element; they cannot be cached; and they beat almost every other rule in the cascade, which makes them hard to override later.

A `<style>` element inside `<head>` holds ordinary CSS rules with selectors. It is the right tool for a single-page demo, for the examples in this tutorial, and for *critical CSS*: a few rules inlined into the page so the first paint does not have to wait for a file download.

blocks.text: The drawback appears as soon as a site has a second page: the rules must be copied into every file, and a change means editing all of them.

For a real site the CSS lives in its own file and every page references it with a `<link>` element in the `<head>`. The browser downloads the file once, caches it, and reuses it for every page that links to it. `rel="stylesheet"` tells the browser what kind of resource it is and `href` says where to find it; no `type` attribute is needed.

blocks.title: When the stylesheet "does not work"
blocks.text: Almost always the `link` element is at fault: `src` instead of `href` (images use `src`, stylesheets use `href`), a missing `rel="stylesheet"`, or a path relative to the wrong folder. Open the *Network* panel in the developer tools and reload: a red 404 next to the CSS file means the path is wrong.

A page can link several files, and the order matters: when two rules have the same specificity, the one the browser reads *later* wins. Teams usually load a reset or base stylesheet first and component styles after it, so component rules can override the base. The same ordering applies between a `<link>` and a `<style>` element: whichever comes later in the document wins ties.

blocks.title: Base first, overrides later
blocks.code:
<head>
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="/css/base.css">
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="/css/components.css">
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="/css/print.css" media="print">
</head>

blocks.text: The optional `media` attribute restricts a stylesheet to a situation; `media="print"` loads the file but applies it only when printing. You will see the same conditions written inside CSS as media queries in [Responsive Design](/tutorials/css/responsive-design).

CSS can also pull in another file with `@import url("reset.css");` at the top of a stylesheet. It works, but the browser only discovers the imported file after downloading the first one, so the two downloads happen one after the other instead of in parallel. Prefer multiple `<link>` elements, or a build tool that combines files.

All three methods feed the same cascade. An inline `style` attribute beats any normal rule from a `<style>` element or a linked file, regardless of order, because the cascade treats it as more specific than any selector; only a declaration marked `!important` can beat it. Between a `<style>` element and a linked stylesheet nothing special happens: they are just rules, resolved by specificity and then by order.

blocks.title: Rule of thumb
blocks.text: External stylesheet for everything that is part of the site, a `<style>` element for single-file demos and critical CSS, inline styles only for values generated at runtime. If you are unsure, use the external file.

questions.question: Where should a `<link rel="stylesheet">` element be placed?
questions.explanation: Stylesheet links belong in the `<head>` so the browser can download and apply them before it renders the body.

questions.question: A rule in a linked stylesheet always overrides an inline `style` attribute on the same element.
questions.explanation: It is the other way round: an inline style attribute beats any ordinary rule from a stylesheet, whatever its selector.
